body_html:
Family meals are the heart of life in most Spanish-speaking homes, and they are a wonderful place to practice. The language at the table is repetitive, friendly and full of small rituals. Learn these Spanish phrases for family dinner and you will be able to join in from the first ¡Buen provecho! to the last coffee of the sobremesa.

Key takeaways
  • Say ¡Buen provecho! before eating and to anyone you pass who is eating.
  • Use ¿Me pasas…? (or ¿Me pasa…? with usted) to ask for dishes.
  • Meal times vary: dinner in Spain can start at 9 or 10 p.m.
  • Don’t rush away: the sobremesa is part of the meal.
{{toc}}

Before the meal

  • ¡A comer! / ¡A cenar! Food’s ready! (Time to eat / have dinner!)
  • ¿Pongo la mesa? Shall I set the table?
  • ¿Dónde me siento? Where shall I sit?
  • ¡Qué bien huele! It smells so good!
  • ¡Buen provecho! / ¡Provecho! Enjoy your meal!

Some families say a short grace before eating. If they do, simply wait quietly and join in the amén if you feel comfortable.

Spanish phrases for family dinner: asking and offering

SpanishEnglish
¿Me pasas la sal, por favor?Could you pass the salt, please?
¿Me pasa el pan?Could you pass the bread? (usted)
¿Quieres más?Do you want more?
Sírvete, sírvete.Help yourself.
¿Puedo repetir?Can I have seconds? (Spain)
¿Me sirves un poquito más?Could you give me a little more?
¿Qué lleva este plato?What’s in this dish?

Complimenting the food

Compliments are expected and appreciated. Use them generously:

  • ¡Está riquísimo! It’s delicious!
  • Le quedó buenísimo. It turned out great. (to the cook, usted)
  • Nunca había probado algo así. I’ve never tried anything like this.
  • ¿Me da la receta? Will you give me the recipe?

For many more ways to praise a meal, see {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Saying no (politely) and saying you’re full

Hosts often insist. A gentle, grateful refusal works best:

  • No, gracias, estoy lleno / llena. No, thanks, I’m full.
  • Estaba delicioso, pero ya no puedo más. It was delicious, but I can’t eat any more.
  • Bueno, un poquito nada más. Okay, just a little bit.
  • Soy alérgico / alérgica a… I’m allergic to…
  • No como carne. I don’t eat meat.
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Toasts and conversation

A simple ¡Salud! (Cheers!) is enough for most toasts. For a special dinner you might say Por la familia (To family) or Por muchos años más juntos (To many more years together). Easy conversation topics include the food, family news, plans and memories: ¿Se acuerdan cuando…? (Do you remember when…?).

After the meal: helping and the sobremesa

  • ¿Te ayudo a recoger? Can I help clear up?
  • Yo lavo los platos. I’ll do the dishes.
  • ¿Alguien quiere café? Does anyone want coffee?

Then comes the sobremesa, the unhurried conversation that lingers at the table after eating. The RAE dictionary defines it as the time spent at the table after a meal, and in many families it lasts longer than the meal itself. Getting up straight away can seem rude; relax and enjoy it. I write more about words like this in {{link:spanish-words-with-no-english-translation|Spanish words with no English translation}}.

Meal times and customs by country

CountryMain mealDinner
Spainla comida, around 2–3 p.m.la cena, often 9–10 p.m.
Mexicola comida, mid-afternoonla cena, often lighter
ArgentinaLunch at middayDinner late, often after 9 p.m.

Note that comida means both “food” and “the main meal of the day”, so ¿Vienes a comer? usually means lunch, not dinner.

A sample dinner conversation

  • Host: ¡A cenar! Siéntate aquí, a mi lado. (Dinner’s ready! Sit here, next to me.)
  • You: Gracias. ¡Qué bien huele! ¡Buen provecho! (Thanks. It smells great! Enjoy!)
  • Host: ¿Quieres más arroz? (Do you want more rice?)
  • You: Sí, un poquito, por favor. Está riquísimo. (Yes, a little, please. It’s delicious.)
  • Host: Es la receta de mi abuela. (It’s my grandmother’s recipe.)
  • You: ¡Con razón! ¿Me la enseña algún día? (No wonder! Will you teach it to me one day?)

When you’re the host

If you invite your partner’s family or friends, a few host phrases help you sound warm and in control:

  • Pasen, pasen, están en su casa. Come in, come in, make yourselves at home.
  • ¿Qué les sirvo de tomar? What can I get you to drink?
  • La cena estará lista en diez minutos. Dinner will be ready in ten minutes.
  • Espero que les guste. Es la primera vez que lo preparo. I hope you like it. It’s the first time I’ve made it.
  • Gracias por venir. Thanks for coming.

Admitting it is your first attempt at a dish usually earns kindness, not criticism.

One more custom worth knowing: in many homes bread stays on the table, not on your plate, and you keep both hands visible above the table rather than in your lap. Small details like these are rarely mentioned, but families notice them.

Common mistakes

  • Saying estoy lleno de + food. Just say estoy lleno / llena.
  • Leaving right after eating. Stay for the sobremesa.
  • Saying la comida es bueno. Comida is feminine: la comida está buena.

Family dinners are one of many everyday moments covered in {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}. If it is your first visit, read {{link:meeting-your-partners-family-in-spanish|meeting your partner’s family in Spanish}} too.

Final thoughts

At a Spanish-speaking family table, the most important phrases are the simplest: buen provecho, está riquísimo and gracias. Say them often, stay for the sobremesa and you will be invited back.

faq.q: What do you say before eating in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Buen provecho! or just ¡Provecho! It means “enjoy your meal” and is said before eating and to people you pass who are eating.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m full” in Spanish?
faq.a: Estoy lleno (male) or estoy llena (female). A polite addition is pero estaba delicioso, “but it was delicious”.
Sobremesa is the time spent talking at the table after a meal. In many Spanish-speaking families it is an important part of the gathering.
